architecture.fell_back_and_why: Followed SKILL.md from step 1. Inventory produced a six-component matrix and staffed six specialists, dispatched in ONE message so they would run in parallel per SKILL.md section 3 and team.md. The harness accepted only the FIRST (ehs-web-api, scoped to fieldops-api + settlement-worker) and rejected the other five with 'Concurrent subagent limit reached. You can run 20 subagents at once. Do not retry.' - the pool was saturated by agents outside this session, so only one slot was ever free. A single re-probe for ehs-mobile alone was also refused. The plugin subagent types (ehs-*) are not registered in this harness either, so team.md's documented fallback path was used: a general-purpose sub-agent instructed to read agents/ehs-web-api.md and follow it verbatim, with ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} substituted. Rather than silently dropping five of six components, the leader ran the remaining five specialist roles IN ITS OWN CONTEXT (mobile, infra-cloud, ai-safety, privacy-abuse, supply-chain), reading each role's pack sections that the inventory justified (mobile.md, mobile-runtime-trust.md section 7, infra-cloud.md, ai-safety.md sections 0-3, ai-safety-data-output.md index, privacy-abuse.md sections 1-3, plus the SUP/INF procedure indexes) and triage.md before writing any finding. Consequence to declare honestly: those five roles did NOT get an independent context, so they lack the context-isolation the skill relies on, and their VER-09 pass was self-administered rather than blind. The one component pair that DID get a separate context (fieldops-api, settlement-worker) is the only part of this report where the blind-critic property of section 8 genuinely holds. One cross-context integration was performed by the leader and is the clearest argument for the architecture: the sub-agent capped its proxy-header authentication bypass at 'probable' because the load-balancer configuration was outside its assigned scope; the leader, holding pulumi-platform, found edge.ts:35 dropInvalidHeaderFields:false with a comment stating the x-fieldops-* headers are deliberately forwarded untouched, which settles FP-08 and promotes that finding to confirmed.

findings.title: Dead-letter drain re-applies messages that were rejected by the signature and scope checks
findings.class: Authorization Bypass Through an Alternate Path

Two of the things that raise there are the controls themselves: decode() raises ValueError('bad producer signature') at consumer.py:72, and _require_scope raises Forbidden at handlers.py:31. findings.title: Load balancer forwards client-supplied x-fieldops-* headers and the API trusts them as an authenticated identity
findings.evidence: auth.ts:59-61: `if (!actor && config.trustProxyIdentity) actor = fromProxyHeaders(c.req.raw.headers)`. fromProxyHeaders (auth.ts:45-53) reads x-fieldops-actor, x-fieldops-org, x-fieldops-role and x-fieldops-crews verbatim, casting role without checking it is one of the four valid values. trustProxyIdentity is true whenever NODE_ENV==='production' (config.ts:28). The fallback is EASIER to trigger than the token path - simply omit the Authorization header. The sub-agent capped this at probable because the balancer config was outside its scope; the leader resolved it from the infrastructure program: pulumi-platform/edge.ts:35 sets dropInvalidHeaderFields:false, with the comment at edge.ts:32-34 stating that the dispatcher fleet's identity 'reaches us as a set of x-fieldops-* headers, so the listener has to pass request headers through to the target group untouched'. The ALB is configured to forward, not to strip or overwrite.
findings.impact: Any internet caller reaching the public listener (network.ts:76, 0.0.0.0/0 on 443) sends x-fieldops-actor and x-fieldops-role: admin with no token and becomes an administrator of any org they name, on every /api/v1/* route.
findings.recommendation: Have the proxy sign what it asserts - an mTLS-derived principal in a signed JWT the API verifies - rather than asserting it in a plaintext header. At minimum set dropInvalidHeaderFields:true, strip x-fieldops-* at the listener, bind the fallback to a shared secret, and validate role against the Role union.

findings.title: The two-leg payout is not atomic, and the surviving leg is then replayed
findings.evidence: _apply_payout posts two independent movements (handlers.py:46 and :55). Each post_entry commits its own Redis WATCH/MULTI/EXEC and then its own Postgres insert on its own connection (ledger.py:59-83); nothing spans the pair. If leg two raises InsufficientFunds (ledger.py:67), leg one's credit to CLEARING_ACCOUNT is already committed, the exception reaches consumer.run_once, the entry is dead-lettered, and the drain calls _apply_payout again - re-crediting the clearing account each cycle. Separately the Redis commit at ledger.py:72 and the journal insert at ledger.py:78 are not in a common transaction, so a crash between them moves money with no audit row, against the module's own claim at ledger.py:4-5.
findings.impact: An attacker who arranges leg two to fail inflates the clearing balance on every drain cycle, because post_entry refuses only negative results. Independently, balances and the audit journal can diverge silently.
findings.recommendation: Make the pair one unit - a Lua script or a single MULTI over both keys - and journal inside the same commit, or write the journal first and reconcile forward.

triage.reason: no transaction, lock or compensating reversal wraps the two post_entry calls; the WATCH at ledger.py:62 covers one key for one call

scope.established_by: traced the commit boundaries of each post_entry call

findings.title: Idempotency is advisory: non-atomic in one handler, absent in two, and the atomic primitive is uncalled
findings.evidence: Three defects on one control. (2) handle_payout_cancel (:91) and handle_payout_reissue (:107) never call lookup at all, so each redelivery re-applies; cancel also credits destination_account without verifying the payout it names was ever applied, so the same cancel replayed N times credits N times. (3) idempotency.claim (:42) - SET NX EX, exactly the atomic guard this needs - and release (:47) have zero callers.
findings.impact: Duplicate stream delivery, which Redis Streams guarantees is possible, moves money more than once on three of the four handlers.
findings.recommendation: Route every handler through claim() before applying, remember() after, release() on failure; give the receipt store a unique constraint in Postgres rather than a Redis TTL.

findings.title: Row-level security is enabled without FORCE, so the owning role the pipeline runs as bypasses every policy
findings.class: Row-Level Security Not Enforced Against the Table Owner
findings.evidence: row_security.sql:18 emits `alter table {{ relation }} enable row level security` with no accompanying FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. In PostgreSQL, ENABLE alone leaves the table owner exempt from all policies. dbt creates and therefore owns these relations, and profiles.yml:32-42 shows the prod target connecting as WAREHOUSE_USER - the same role that owns the objects. apply_grants.sql:25-26 then grants insert and update on every relation to settlement_app and warehouse_loader on top. The policy itself (row_security.sql:22-24) is otherwise sound and fails closed, since current_setting('app.tenant_id', true) returns NULL when unset and tenant_id = NULL matches nothing.
findings.impact: The tenant_isolation policy the macro exists to install does not constrain the pipeline role or any other owner-equivalent principal, so the isolation the module docstring promises - 'a tenant's session can only ever address its own rows' - holds only for non-owner readers.
findings.recommendation: Emit `alter table ... force row level security` alongside the enable, and confirm that the role reading on behalf of tenants is neither the owner nor a superuser.

triage.reason: no other layer restores the constraint for the owner; apply_grants.sql adds privileges rather than removing them

the assertion is that the emitted DDL omits FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, established by reading row_security.sql:18, and PostgreSQL's exemption of the table owner under ENABLE alone is documented behaviour rather than a deployment fact. Whether the tenant-facing reader is ALSO the owner changes how much the omission costs, which is stated in the impact, and is not an exculpation of the omission
the reading is a documented PostgreSQL behaviour: ENABLE exempts the owner, FORCE does not
the omission applies to every relation the macro is run against - all of staging and marts per dbt_project.yml:32,40

scope.established_by: read the emitted DDL statement by statement and compared it against what PostgreSQL requires for owner enforcement
scope.narrowed_by: the policy predicate itself fails closed for non-owner roles, so non-owner readers are correctly isolated; how far the owner exemption reaches depends on the deployed grant state, which is outside this repository

findings.title: Deterministic pseudonym is an unsalted hash of the customer id, reversible by enumeration
findings.evidence: mask_pii.sql:33 encode(digest(customer_id || 'v3', 'sha256'), 'hex') - the only entropy added to the identifier is var('pii_policy_version'), which is the literal v3 declared in plain text at dbt_project.yml:18 and therefore not a secret. models/marts/schema.yml:44-46 describes the output as a 'Stable hash, safe to join on across environments'.

The pseudonym re-identifies rather than de-identifies, and because it is stable across environments the same value links records in lower environments back to production subjects.
findings.recommendation: Key the digest with a secret held outside the repository (HMAC with a warehouse-side key), or use a random surrogate stored in a mapping table with restricted access; do not treat a version string as a salt.

findings.title: max_delivery_attempts is configured but never read, so a single exception dead-letters a message immediately
findings.evidence: settings.py:51 declares max_delivery_attempts with a default of 5 and the consumer docstring at consumer.py:5-6 states that failures 'go to the dead-letter stream after max_delivery_attempts'. A search of both assigned trees finds the symbol only in that declaration and that docstring - there is no reader. consumer.run_once at consumer.py:112-117 catches the first exception of any kind and dead-letters the entry on the spot.
findings.impact: The documented retry budget does not exist: one transient database timeout, and equally one signature rejection or one authorization failure, promotes a message straight into the dead-letter stream. This is the mechanism the dead-letter replay bypass depends on, since it is what puts a REJECTED message where the drain will re-apply it.
findings.recommendation: Honour the retry budget by tracking delivery count (XAUTOCLAIM or the entry's delivery counter) before dead-lettering, and send control-rejected messages to a separate quarantine stream the drain refuses.

triage.reason: a reader could exist in a deployment wrapper or supervisor outside the two assigned components; both trees were grepped and only the declaration and the docstring were found, and per FP-08 absence of that artifact is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS. This is what caps the finding at probable
the value is an ordinary dataclass field, not consumed by reflection or by a settings struct read wholesale
